terms.gloss: a pole or long staff: the pole to hold on to
evidence: Plin. NH 15.11: perticīs oleās dēcutere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical word for a pole or a long staff (Lewis & Short), and Traupman’s word for a pole (p. 49). Its use for the pole one holds on to in a bus or a metro carriage is modern, and ours: Traupman and Morgan–Owens have no word for it.

Classically a column, pillar or post (Lewis & Short). Our use of it for the pole in a carriage, which is a fixed upright as a pillar is; the perticae of the authors are mostly loose poles held in the hand.

phrases.latin: Cum nūlla sēdēs vacua esset, stābant, Theodōrus columnam tenēns, ut virī solent.
phrases.english: As no seat was free, they stood, Theo holding the pole, as men do.

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 49.
